title: Tiny Snakes Cartwheel Away From Danger
paragraphs: It sounds like a cartoon, but it is now documented in a peer-reviewed journal: a group of tiny snakes from Southeast Asia escapes by cartwheeling. A study in Current Biology, led by Yosuke Kojima of Toho University in Japan, sets out how dwarf reed snakes, hardly longer than a ruler, pull it off.

Filming 13 snakes of the genus Pseudorabdion from Kubah National Park in Malaysia on a narrow track, the researchers found that every individual rolled when given a gentle tap, while six snakes of the genus Calamaria, used as a comparison group, stayed on the ground. Each roll is driven by a "stroke": one flank is whipped towards the ground as an arched section of the body swings down beside the head, and the snake switches sides with every cycle. The pay-off is a speed roughly four times that of ordinary slithering, achieved while the head remains remarkably steady and keeps facing forward.

Caution is warranted, however. The rolling was induced by prodding in a laboratory rather than by predators, the sample is small, and the evolutionary origin of the trick is unexplained. Kojima concedes that the movement may be costly: "This mode of locomotion may require a lot of energy, but we don't yet know how long the snakes can sustain it."

questions.q: Why should the results be treated with caution?
questions.a: The rolling was induced in a laboratory, and the sample was small.

questions.q: What role did the Calamaria snakes play?
questions.a: They were the comparison group, and none of them rolled.

questions.q: What does the word "stroke" refer to in the study?
questions.a: A repeated movement in which one side of the body is whipped towards the ground while an arched section swings down.
